# Research Memorandum: Independent Criticism and Alternative Explanations

## Scope and Method

This memorandum covers file pages 465 through 509 of *Learnability and Cognition: The Acquisition of Argument Structure*. The section is almost entirely apparatus: endnotes to chapters 4 through 7 running from file page 465 to file page 475, the reference list from file page 476 to file page 495, and the index from file page 496 to file page 509. I say this plainly because the user asked me not to pad. There is no new argumentative prose here. The notes are not neutral, however. They contain qualifications, admissions of uncertainty, alternative analyses, and explicit concessions that the main text sometimes glosses over. Those are exactly the material an independent critic needs. I treat them as evidence and cite file pages only. I do not cite printed page labels. I do not cite anything outside this section. Where a claim depends on a figure or diagram, I say so; no figures appear in this extraction.

My assigned job is independent criticism and alternative explanations. I try to defeat the provisional theory using what Steven Pinker actually says here. I keep Pinker's claims separate from our engineering proposals. I do not assume that a non-neural machine is what Pinker argues for; he argues about human language acquisition, and the substrate question is not addressed in this section. I do not treat linguistic findings as universal laws of learning. Where the source is silent, I say so.

## The Strongest Challenge: Motivated Categories Do Not Predict Class Membership, So Any Theory That Learns Classes From Semantic Motivation Alone Will Overgenerate

Note 4 to chapter 4 is the single most damaging passage in this section for the provisional theory. Pinker reports that he shares Maratsos's doubts about Lakoff's motivated categories. He observes that judgments of well-formedness or ill-formedness of class members are "often much more discriminating than the best 'motivation' one can discover," that speakers reject many putative members that are as well motivated as those already in a category, and that motivations cannot be predicted in advance, not by the linguist and therefore presumably not by the learner (file page 465). His conclusion is stark: motivated classes must be learned as lists at least part of the time (file page 465).

This is a direct hit on "bounded deterministic program construction over calibrated sensor records without supplied circle or square definitions." If the machine discovers a semantic motivation for a class and then admits every candidate satisfying that motivation, it will overgenerate exactly the way Pinker says human learners do not. The provisional theory has no notion of listing as a partial brake. It also has no account of the fact that the motivation itself is often invisible to the learner.

**Discriminating task.** Give the machine a set of event types with a discoverable semantic motivation for grouping, plus a handful of exceptions that share the motivation but are rejected by the target grammar. Ask it to predict which novel items belong. If it admits the exceptions, it is learning motivation rather than class membership. If it blocks them without witnessing the blocking, it has a mechanism the source does not supply and that mechanism needs to be named.

## The Second Challenge: The Provisional Theory Has No Account of Idiosyncratic Means, and Pinker Shows These Block Generalization

Note 20 to chapter 4 lists "harmless positive exceptions" to causative generalizations: one can rattle something only by shaking it, secrets but not water can be leaked, pipes but not poorly dyed clothing can be bled, cigarettes and ham can be smoked but firewood and butter cannot, and transitive shine can only mean "polish" or "direct a beam" (file page 467). Note 21 adds that anticausativization applies only to causative verbs that could have been formed from a causativization rule to begin with, excluding verbs with lexical specification of direction, manner of causation, or motion of an instrument (file page 468). Note 13 to chapter 5 makes the same point about sink: transitive sink is not the product of a causativization rule but an independent verb specifying a means of causation, roughly "cause to sink in water by means of causing to be full of water" (file page 471).

The provisional theory says it "composes elementary operations and previously constructed subprograms." Nothing in that formulation distinguishes a verb that specifies only an effect from a verb that specifies an effect plus a means. Yet Pinker's analysis turns on exactly this distinction. Without it, the machine will causativize verbs it should not and will fail to block forms that native speakers reject.

**Discriminating intervention.** Present the machine with pairs of change-of-state verbs matched for effect but differing in whether the means of causation is lexically specified. Ask it to generate transitive forms. If it treats both members of each pair alike, the composition mechanism is missing the means specification. If it distinguishes them, the specification must be in the representational vocabulary from the start, which is a hidden answer.

## The Third Challenge: The Constraint That Makes the Learning Account Work Is Stipulated, Not Derived

Note 5 to chapter 6 is the clearest admission in this section. Pinker says he will use cognitive considerations to motivate a constraint, "necessary for the current learning account to work," that object properties of locative verbs are attached to the theme argument in the motion structure and not to the patient argument in the action structure (file page 472 through 473). He gives reasons: the properties of an object loaded into a container must be appropriate to the container, and the fact that sprayed stuff is liquid is intimately related to the shape it assumes while moving (file page 472 through 473). But the constraint is doing load-bearing work and is justified after the fact.

For the provisional theory this is fatal in a specific way. "Calibrated sensor records" do not come with an instruction about which argument a property binds to. If the binding is supplied, the learning claim is weakened. If it is not supplied, the learning account does not work, by Pinker's own statement.

**Discriminating task.** Give the machine observations of loading and spraying events with shape and material properties visible but no labels for theme or patient. Ask it to predict which properties constrain which argument in a novel alternation. If it can do this without a supplied binding convention, the provisional theory has found something Pinker's account requires but does not derive. If it cannot, the binding is hidden in the design.

## The Fourth Challenge: Rule Creation May Need to Encode Inference Premises, Which Compounds the Search Problem

Note 6 to chapter 6 raises a problem Pinker himself flags as possibly problematic. For the stuff verbs, the state of the with-variant may be related to the manner of the into-variant not by copying identical structures but by a kind of cognitive inference: inserting contents against resistance in the into form is related to the container being overfull in the with form (file page 473). If so, the rule-creation process would have to include in the rule not only the parts of the input structure coindexed with alternating arguments but also any parts necessary as premises for the inference of structures in the derivation of the second form (file page 473).

This is an admission that the rule may have to carry inferential baggage. The provisional theory's "bounded deterministic program construction" has no representation for inference premises inside a rule. Adding them enlarges the hypothesis space at exactly the point where the previous memorandum already showed convergence is doubtful.

**Discriminating intervention.** Present the machine with stuff-verb alternations where the two forms are related by inference rather than shared structure. Measure whether the learned rule transfers to a novel verb with the same inferential relation. If it does, the rule must contain something beyond structural copying. If it does not, the theory has deferred the problem.

## The Fifth Challenge: The Provisional Theory's Episode Records Are Not Enough; Pinker Needs Aspectual and Time-Line Structure

Note 3 to chapter 6 says Pinker has not dealt with the aspectual or time-line representation in discussing the learning procedures, but assumes that broad-range and narrow-range rules include them, perhaps with only a coarse point-and-region distinction for the former (file page 472). Note 7 adds that the importance of aspectual differences is consistent with Tenny's proposal that aspect is a key interface between lexical semantics and syntax (file page 473). Note 25 to chapter 4 goes further, suggesting that aspectual operations apply to the temporal properties of the role played by the surface subject argument, and that it is harder to expand the temporal unfolding of a patient's change of state than of an agent's action (file page 468 through 469).

The provisional theory's "episode-specific records" are a start, but they are not the same thing as an aspectual representation that grammatical rules can inspect. A record of what happened is not a representation of how the event unfolds in time relative to a reference point. Without the latter, the machine cannot explain why the progressive of an instantaneous state-change verb is better in the active than in the passive.

**Discriminating task.** Give the machine events matched for participants and outcome but differing in whether the change is instantaneous or extended. Ask it to generate progressive forms in active and passive voice. If it distinguishes them, it has aspectual structure beyond raw episode records. If it does not, temporal memory is a shortcut rather than a mechanism.

## The Sixth Challenge: Positive Exceptions Are Learnable Only Because They Are Positive, Which Restates the Problem

Note 20 says the exceptions are "harmless both because they are positive, hence learnable" (file page 467). This is true but circular for a machine that must discover what to generalize from. The provisional theory proposes to seek observations on which candidate models disagree. That is a good experimental-design principle, but it does not tell the machine which positive instances are exceptions and which are exemplary. Pinker's answer is that idiosyncratic meaning elements force individual learning (file page 467). The machine needs a way to detect idiosyncrasy before it has learned the generalization, which is the bootstrapping problem again.

## Alternative Mechanisms the Source Leaves Open

The reference list shows that Pinker engages with, but does not rule out, several alternatives. He cites Michalski and Stepp on conceptual clustering (file page 490), McClelland and Kawamoto on parallel distributed processing (file page 490), Schank on conceptualizations underlying natural language (file page 493), and Marr and Vaina on representation and recognition of shape movement (file page 490). The index records connectionist models and parallel distributed processing as topics (file page 498, file page 505). Nothing in this section argues that these are impossible; the arguments against specific models appear in the main text, not here.

The index also records "scripts" alongside Schank (file page 506), and "semantic representation, autonomy of" as a separate topic (file page 507). Both suggest that Pinker's framework is compatible with structured representations that are not identical to his own formalism. A constraint-satisfaction architecture, a case-based reasoner using stored episodes, or a production system with explicit memory of past applications all remain open on this evidence.

## What the Source Does Not Establish

This section is apparatus. It does not establish that any mechanism suffices for perception, motor control, reasoning about possible actions, or consciousness. Pinker does not claim sentience anywhere here. The provisional theory's refusal to claim consciousness is correct and should be maintained. The notes are about verb semantics and argument structure in natural language. They do not generalize to a theory of thinking.

## Engineering Implications, Clearly Marked as Our Proposals

The following are our extensions, not Pinker's claims.

First, the machine needs a representation that distinguishes effect-only specifications from effect-plus-means specifications, because the source shows that this distinction blocks or licenses generalization.

Second, the machine needs a binding convention for properties of moved objects, and it must be explicit about whether that convention is supplied or learned. Pinker says the learning account requires it (file page 472 through 473).

Third, the machine needs aspectual structure that rules can inspect, not merely timestamped episode records.

Fourth, the machine needs a notion of listedness or idiosyncrasy detection that operates before the generalization is fully formed, or it will overgenerate motivated classes.

Fifth, the machine needs a representation for inferential premises inside rules if it is to handle cases like the stuff verbs (file page 473).

## Unresolved Questions

The next reader should address whether the reference list entries for Marr and Vaina on shape movement (file page 490) and Michalski and Stepp on conceptual clustering (file page 490) point to mechanisms that could replace Pinker's parameterization approach, or whether they are merely cited foils. The index entry for "maturation, role of" (file page 503) and "sufficient similarity" (file page 506) suggest open questions about when learning windows close and what counts as similar enough to generalize; neither is resolved here. The index entry for "uniqueness as a surrogate for negative evidence" (file page 505) is a mechanism the provisional theory does not use and should be examined. Finally, the relationship between "listed objects/listemes" (file page 504) and the machine's distinction between episode records and reusable knowledge is entirely unaddressed in the provisional theory and is fundamental to any architecture that claims to learn from positive evidence alone.
